training-zone.short: A band of intensity (of power, pace, heart rate or effort) used to plan and log training. Each zone should bring about a similar response in the body for everyone in it.

three-zone-model.short: Splitting intensity at the two thresholds: zone 1 below the first (LT1 or VT1), zone 2 between them, zone 3 above the second (LT2, the respiratory compensation point or critical power).

training-intensity-distribution.short: How an athlete's training is shared out between intensity zones over weeks or months, for example 80% in zone 1, 10% in zone 2 and 10% in zone 3.

pyramidal-training.short: A training intensity distribution with the most training in zone 1, less in zone 2 and the least in zone 3: each step up in intensity gets a smaller share.

threshold-training.short: A training intensity distribution where zone 2 (between the two thresholds) gets the largest share. Also used for single sessions near the second threshold.

time-in-zone.short: Counting training by the minutes actually spent in each zone (from heart rate, power or pace), so a 2 h ride with 20 min of intervals counts mostly as zone 1.

session-goal-method.short: Counting training by sessions: each session goes into the zone of its hardest planned part, so a 2 h ride with 20 min of intervals counts as one zone 3 session.

polarisation-index.short: A single number for how polarised a training distribution is: log₁₀(zone 1 ÷ zone 2 × zone 3 × 100), with each zone as a fraction of training. Above 2.00 counts as polarised.

survivorship-bias.short: A mistake from looking only at those who succeeded: copying what champions did ignores the many who did the same and never became champions.

standardised-mean-difference.short: The difference between two groups' average changes divided by the spread of the data, so studies using different tests can be pooled. About 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.

network-meta-analysis.short: A meta-analysis that compares several options at once (for example three training plans), even ones never tested head to head, by linking all the trials that share a comparison.

pedro-scale.short: A 10-point checklist of how well a trial was run (random allocation, blinding, follow-up and so on). Higher is better; 4–5 out of 10 means fair to poor.

subgroup-analysis.short: Splitting the people in a study or meta-analysis into groups (for example recreational and competitive) and checking the result in each. Useful for ideas, but easily misleading by chance.

sweet-spot-training.short: A cyclists' name for riding in upper zone 2, just below critical power or FTP: hard enough to be a real stimulus, easy enough to hold for a long time.
